title: startup warmup probes - jordan
content:
Purpose
This is a personal scratchpad to capture small-scale experiments around cold-start / warmup behavior in the runtime. Goal: identify how many requests/tokens until steady-state throughput and where the dominant overheads are (tokenization, model init, kernel warmup, KV cache fill, first-attention pass). Not a polished doc — quick notes for follow-ups and for the SRE/Optimize teams.

Experimental setup (quick)
- Host: dedicated test cluster (single node) with 1x A100-40GB (driver: CUDA 11.8) and a small multi-tenant node with H100 for comparison.
- Runtime build: main@2024-10-31 + warmup-fixes branch (local flags: --kv-cache-enabled --prefill-opt=on).
- Models: small-medium Llama-like: redwood/llm-7b-fp16 (baseline), redwood/llm-7b-int8 (quantized probe).
- Client: curl + small Python harness (requests with keepalive). Each trial is 30s of steady pinging after a cold start (node restart) or process restart.
- Prometheus + nvtop + nsys traces for one hot run.

Measurements captured
- t0: time to first byte (TTFB) for first request after process start (ms)
- t_first_token: latency for the first generated token (ms)
- tokens_per_sec (steady-state): measured from 10s-30s window
- kernel-warmup: observed increased GPU SM utilization during first 2-4 requests
- cpu-overhead: tokenization and request prep (ms) measured client-side

Run summary (selected trials)
1) Fresh process start (no prior requests), 1 request at a time, seq_len=64, batch=1
- model: llm-7b-fp16 on A100
- TTFB: 480 ms
- first_token: 510 ms
- steady tokens/sec: 150 tok/s
- GPU util first 10s: 18% -> steady 42%
- Notes: first request dominated by JIT/kernels + cuBLAS workspace alloc. nvprof shows kernel compilation-ish overhead (dynamic kernel selection + small workspace).

2) Same as (1) but after one warm request (warm cache)
- TTFB: 120 ms
- first_token: 135 ms
- steady tokens/sec: 160 tok/s (small improvement)
- GPU util: 45% steady
- Notes: major improvement in TTFB; suggests init/alloc cost amortized. Slight throughput bump too.

3) Cold node restart (OS-level), same model
- TTFB: 1.3s (first request)
- first_token: 1.5s
- steady tokens/sec: 140 tok/s
- Observations: node-level restart incurs device reinitialization + driver context setup. Persistent processes avoid this.

4) Quantized model (int8), cold process start
- TTFB: 720 ms
- first_token: 760 ms
- steady tokens/sec: 210 tok/s
- Notes: higher first request cost vs fp16 but much higher steady throughput. Quantization changed kernel paths and increased small-kernel initialization time.

5) Small burst test (5 quick seq=128 requests, batch=1, 50ms inter-request)
- First three requests: per-request latency ~600-800ms; after request 4 latency stabilizes ~380ms; tokens/sec observed jump after cache fills (prefill + kv cache)
- Conclusion: KV cache warmup matters for repeated sequences with overlapping context.

Micro-observations / hypothesis
- Two distinct warmup costs: 1) process/node startup (allocs/drivers), 2) first few model inferences (kernel selection + cuBLAS workspace + small-tensor kernel launches).
- Tokenization (CPU) adds ~15-25 ms per request in our harness for English text; not dominant for long sequences, but significant for short prompt + short generation cases.
- Quantized kernels incur extra per-kernel setup cost but better steady-state throughput. This explains larger delta between first request and steady throughput for int8.
- Keep-alive connections cut ~100-300ms off TTFB vs cold client TCP/TLS handshakes in our test infra.

Quick list of commands used (for reproducibility)
- start server: ./serve --model llm-7b-fp16 --listen :8080 --enable-kv-cache
- client perf: python perf_probe.py --model llm-7b-fp16 --seq 64 --duration 30 --batch 1 --keepalive
- simple curl check: curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/generate -d '{"prompt":"hello world","max_tokens":64}' | jq '.latency'

Representative ascii table (first-run vs warmed)
- headers: scenario | TTFB(ms) | first_token(ms) | steady_tok_s
- rows:
  fresh-process | 480 | 510 | 150
  warmed-process | 120 | 135 | 160
  node-restart | 1300 | 1500 | 140
  int8-fresh | 720 | 760 | 210

Open questions / next probes
- Is kernel selection cacheable across model versions? Try minor weight bit flips or re-quantized variants to see if we pay warm kernel penalty again.
- Measure impact of increasing batch size on warmup delta (1,2,4,8). Do bigger batches reduce per-token warm penalty?
- Profile memory alloc patterns to confirm workspace allocations are the bulk of first-request delta. Could preallocate workspaces at process start to reduce TTFB.
- Repeat on H100 multi-tenant node to see if driver/multi-process context sharing reduces node-restart penalty.

Action items (quick)
- [ ] Add an opt-in early workspace prealloc flag in serving runtime to evaluate savings (issue tracked: SERVE-2202).
- [ ] Run batch-size sweep (1-8) with warm vs cold runs, log deltas (assign: Evan).
- [ ] Measure tokenization-only overhead with local script (assign: Aisha).
- [ ] Convert a short note into a Confluence page summarizing recommended mitigations for app teams (after we have batch sweep).

Notes to self
- This lives as a user scratchpad; move to shared doc if we want to present to runtime owners. Keep small numbers reproducible. Save raw traces under /tmp/warmup-traces-Jordan-2024-11 (done).

Bottom line (rough):
- Cold process/node starts can add order-of-magnitude to first-request latency (hundreds ms to >1s).
- After 2-3 requests steady-state behavior is reached for FP16; quantized paths warm slower but deliver higher throughput.
- Simple mitigations to try: keepalive / persistent processes, preallocate workspaces, and small warmup probes at process start.

-- Jordan
